fixed.q: In the von Neumann architecture:
o: Program and data share the same memory
Program and data have separate memories
Only data is stored in memory
fixed.w: Harvard architecture uses separate instruction and data memories.

fixed.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be executed?
fixed.w: IR holds the current instruction; MAR holds the memory address being accessed; MDR/MBR holds the data.

fixed.q: The ALU and control unit together form the:
A system with a 16-bit address bus can address how many memory locations?
fixed.w: n address lines → 2ⁿ locations.

fixed.q: Which flag is set when the result of an operation is zero?
fixed.w: Overflow flag: signed result out of range.

fixed.q: In immediate addressing mode, the operand is:
o: At the address given in the instruction
At the address held in a register
fixed.w: Direct: instruction holds the operand's address. Indirect: instruction holds the address of the address. Register indirect: register holds the address.

fixed.q: Which addressing mode needs two memory accesses to get the operand (besides fetching the instruction)?
fixed.w: Fetch the effective address, then the operand.

fixed.q: Relative (PC-relative) addressing is mainly used for:
fixed.w: EA = PC + offset. Indexed addressing is used for arrays; base register for relocation.

fixed.q: Which addressing mode is best for accessing array elements?
fixed.w: EA = base address + index register.

fixed.q: A zero-address instruction format is used by a:
fixed.w: One-address: accumulator. Two/three-address: general registers.

fixed.q: Which is a characteristic of RISC processors?
fixed.w: RISC: few simple instructions, many registers, hardwired control, pipelining-friendly. CISC: complex, variable length, microprogrammed.

fixed.q: Compared with microprogrammed control, hardwired control is:
fixed.w: Microprogrammed control stores control words in control memory (flexible).

fixed.q: In a microprogrammed control unit, microinstructions are stored in:
fixed.w: Horizontal microcode: one bit per control signal (wide, fast). Vertical: encoded (narrow, needs decoding).

fixed.q: Arrange in increasing access speed: main memory, registers, cache, disk.
fixed.w: Faster memory is costlier and smaller.

fixed.q: Cache memory works on the principle of:
fixed.w: Temporal (reuse soon) and spatial (nearby addresses).

fixed.q: Which cache mapping allows a block to be placed only in one specific cache line?
fixed.w: Fully associative: any line. k-way set associative: any line in one set.

fixed.q: A direct-mapped cache has 128 lines of 16 bytes and memory is 64 KB (16-bit address). The tag, line and offset bits are:
fixed.w: Offset = log₂16 = 4; line = log₂128 = 7; tag = 16 − 11 = 5.

fixed.q: Average memory access time with hit ratio h, cache time tc and memory time tm (hierarchical access) is:
fixed.w: Simultaneous access: h·tc + (1 − h)·tm.

fixed.q: Which memory loses its contents when power is switched off?
fixed.w: SRAM (flip-flops, faster, used for cache) vs DRAM (capacitors, needs refresh, main memory).

fixed.q: Cache memory is usually built from:
In write-through cache policy:
o: Every write updates both cache and main memory
Memory is updated only when the block is replaced
fixed.w: Write-back uses a dirty bit and updates memory on replacement.

fixed.q: The speedup of a k-stage pipeline executing n instructions (compared with no pipelining) is:
fixed.w: Pipelined time = (k + n − 1) cycles vs nk unpipelined. As n → ∞ the speedup approaches k (the maximum/ideal speedup).

fixed.q: A pipeline hazard caused by an instruction needing the result of a previous one is a:
fixed.w: Structural: resource conflict. Control: branches. Data hazards are reduced by operand forwarding.

fixed.q: Branch prediction is used to reduce:
DMA (Direct Memory Access) transfers data:
o: Between I/O and memory without involving the CPU for each word
fixed.w: Modes: burst, cycle stealing, transparent. The CPU only sets up the transfer.

fixed.q: In which I/O method does the CPU repeatedly check the device status?
fixed.w: Interrupt-driven I/O frees the CPU until the device signals.

fixed.q: An interrupt that cannot be ignored or disabled by the CPU is:
fixed.w: Vectored interrupts supply the address of the ISR.

fixed.q: Booth's algorithm is used for:
fixed.w: Restoring/non-restoring algorithms are for division.

fixed.q: In IEEE 754 single precision, the exponent bias is:
fixed.w: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa. Double: 11-bit exponent, bias 1023.

fixed.q: Which bus carries the address of a memory location from the CPU?
Memory that does not change its contents due to external causes is referred to as:
fixed.w: Static memory keeps its contents unless deliberately changed.

fixed.q: Which of the following is NV RAM memory that retains its data even when turned off?
fixed.w: Flash memory is non-volatile RAM-like memory that keeps data without power.

fixed.q: The semiconductor memory Dynamic RAM (DRAM) stores each bit of information in a/an ______.
fixed.w: DRAM stores each bit as charge on a capacitor, which needs refreshing; SRAM uses flip-flops.

fixed.q: A four-way set-associative cache memory unit with a capacity of 32 KB is built using a block size of 1 K. The word length is 8 bits. The size of the physical address space is 32 GB. The number of bits for the TAG field is:
fixed.w: 32 GB = 2³⁵ addresses. Offset = 10 bits (1 K block); 32 KB/1 K = 32 blocks/4 ways = 8 sets, so 3 index bits. TAG = 35 − 10 − 3 = 22.

fixed.q: Select the option that best describes the truthfulness of the following statements. i) RAM is a volatile memory having a limited storage capacity. ii) Secondary memory is storage other than the RAM and ROM.
fixed.w: RAM is volatile with limited capacity, and secondary memory is storage other than RAM and ROM. Both true.

fixed.q: How many address lines and input-output data line are needed for the 64k × 8 memory unit?
fixed.w: 64K = 2¹⁶ words needs 16 address lines, and an 8-bit word needs 8 data lines.

fixed.q: A 26-bit address bus has a maximum accessible memory capacity of ____.
fixed.w: 2^26 bytes = 2^6 × 2^20 = 64 MB (byte-addressable).

fixed.q: A computer has a single cache (off-chip) with a 3 ns hit time and a 95% hit rate. Main memory has a 50 ns access time. If we add an on-chip cache with a 0.6 ns hit time and a 98% hit rate, the computer's effective access time is:
fixed.w: Off-chip level: 3 + 0.05 × 50 = 5.5 ns. With the on-chip cache in front: 0.6 + 0.02 × 5.5 = 0.71 ≈ 0.7 ns.

fixed.q: In the construction of which of the following components are bipolar devices desirable?
fixed.w: Bipolar (TTL/ECL) devices are fast but costly and power-hungry, so they suit small, speed-critical memories: cache and control (microprogram) memory.

fixed.q: The principle of locality of reference justifies the use of
fixed.w: Locality of reference is the reason a small, fast cache gives a high hit rate.

fixed.q: Spatial locality refers to the problem that once a location is referenced
o: It will not be referenced again
A nearby location will be referenced soon
fixed.w: Spatial locality means nearby addresses will be used soon. "Referenced again" describes temporal locality.

fixed.q: Which of the following statements is not true?
o: Caching holds output for a device.
Caching transparently stores data in a component called a cache, so that future requests for that data can be served faster.
Data stored in a cache may be a previously computed value or a duplicate of an original value stored elsewhere.
fixed.w: Holding output for a device is buffering or spooling, not caching.

fixed.q: Which level of RAID refers to disk mirroring with block striping?
fixed.w: Korth defines RAID level 1 as "disk mirroring with block striping" (often called RAID 1+0 or 10).

fixed.q: Which of the following is not a form of main memory?
fixed.w: An opcode is part of an instruction, not a memory. Caches, registers and the TLB are all storage.

fixed.q: The group of digits stored at each address in memory is generally referred to as
fixed.w: The group of bits stored at one address is a memory word.

fixed.q: RAID configuration of disks is used to provide
fixed.w: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) mainly provides fault tolerance through redundancy. Some levels also improve speed.

fixed.q: Which of the following is an example of nonvolatile memory?
fixed.w: ROM is non-volatile.

fixed.q: Which of the following part of the CPU has the necessary electronic circuitry to perform binary addition and shift operations in computer system?
fixed.w: The ALU contains the circuits for arithmetic (binary addition) and shift/logic operations.

fixed.q: In CPU, which of the following type of register is required by the control unit and contains the instruction currently being executed?
fixed.w: The instruction register (IR) holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.

fixed.q: A computer bus line is made up of which of the following components?
fixed.w: A bus is a set of parallel lines (address, data and control).

fixed.q: What is the size of the computer accumulator register?
fixed.w: 4 bytes. Accumulator size depends on the CPU's word length (32-bit = 4 bytes).

fixed.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of computer architecture?
fixed.w: Micro-architecture, Harvard and ISA are computer architectures; software architecture is a software-design concept.

fixed.q: The mask logical micro operation is equivalent to which logical gate?
fixed.w: A mask (selective-clear) operation ANDs the bits with a mask, so it is an AND gate.

fixed.q: Which of the following units can be used to measure the speed of a computer?
fixed.w: MIPS (million instructions per second) and FLOPS (floating-point operations per second) measure processing speed. Baud measures signalling rate on a line, not CPU speed.

fixed.q: Which of the following statements is true?
o: The stack works on the LIFO principle.
PC points to the last instruction that was executed.
fixed.w: ROM is read-only, the PC points to the next instruction, and many instructions (for example MOV) don't affect flags. A stack is last-in, first-out.

fixed.q: The CPU fetches instructions from memory according to the value of the
fixed.w: The PC holds the address of the next instruction to fetch.

fixed.q: A microprogrammed control unit
o: Is faster than a hardwired unit
Facilitates easy implementation of a new instruction
Is useful when small programs are to be run
fixed.w: Microprogramming is slower than hardwired control but flexible: new instructions just need new microcode.

fixed.q: Which of the following is characteristic of a RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) processor?
o: Instruction that manipulate operands in memory
A large number (typically from 100 to 250) of instructions
fixed.w: RISC uses fixed-length, easily decoded instructions, hardwired control, few instructions and register-to-register operations.

fixed.q: In which of the following type of addressing mode, the instruction specifies a register in the CPU whose contents give the address of the operand in memory?
fixed.w: In register-indirect mode the register holds the memory address of the operand.

fixed.q: Which of the following Instruction format use an implied accumulator (AC) register for all data manipulation?
fixed.w: One-address instructions use an implied accumulator for all data manipulation, e.g. ADD X means AC ← AC + M[X].

fixed.q: Which architecture is the most energy efficient?
fixed.w: RISC's simple, fixed-length instructions and fewer transistors make it the most energy-efficient, which is why ARM dominates mobiles.

fixed.q: Which of the following is an addressing mode used in an instruction of the form ADD R1, [R2]?
fixed.w: [R2] means the register holds the operand's address, which is register indirect.

fixed.q: This instruction is of what type? ADD R1, A, B
fixed.w: ADD R1, A, B names three operands (R1 ← A + B), so it is a three-address instruction.

fixed.q: How many memory references are required to fetch an operand in indirect addressing?
fixed.w: In indirect addressing, one memory access fetches the operand's address and a second fetches the operand, so 2 references.

fixed.q: Which of the following addressing modes performs better for accessing an array?
fixed.w: Indexed addressing (base + index register) steps through array elements efficiently.

fixed.q: A register or main memory location that contains the effective address of an operand is known as a
fixed.w: A location that holds an address rather than data is a pointer. This is the idea behind register-indirect and memory-indirect addressing.

fixed.q:
Match List I with List II.
List I: A. 0-address instruction, B. 1-address instruction, C. 2-address instruction, D. 3-address instruction

List II: 1. T = TOP(T − 1), 2. Y = Y + X, 3. Y = A − B, 4. ACC = ACC − X

Codes (A B C D):
fixed.w: 0-address works on the stack top (1). 1-address uses the implied accumulator (4). 2-address is Y = Y + X (2). 3-address is Y = A − B (3). So A-1, B-4, C-2, D-3.

fixed.q: In Direct Memory Access (DMA) ______, a block sequence consisting of a number of memory words is transferred in a continuous burst.
fixed.w: In burst-transfer DMA, a block of words is transferred in one continuous burst while the DMA controller holds the bus.

fixed.q: What would you call the following arrangement? Device P has a cable that plugs into device Q, device Q has a cable that plugs into device R, and device R plugs into a port on the computer.
fixed.w: Devices connected one after another in series form a daisy chain.

fixed.q: Which of the following statements is true?
o: A controller is a collection of electronics that can operate a port, a bus or a device.
A driver is a collection of electronics that can operate a port, a bus or a device.
A host is a collection of electronics that can operate a port, a bus or a device.
A bus is a collection of electronics that can operate a port, a bus or a device.
fixed.w: This is the textbook definition of a controller. A driver is software, not electronics.

fixed.q: Which of the following registers is written by the host to send output?
fixed.w: The host writes the data-out register to send output. It reads the data-in register to get input.

fixed.q: A DMA controller is connected to the
fixed.w: The DMA controller sits on the system bus alongside the CPU and memory.

fixed.q: Which of the following architecture(s) is/are not suitable for realising SIMD?
fixed.w: Von Neumann is a SISD design (one instruction stream, one data stream). Vector and array processors are the classic SIMD machines.

theory.Basics:
• Von Neumann: shared memory for program and data (Harvard: separate).
• PC = next instruction address; IR = current instruction; MAR = address; MDR = data; accumulator.
• n address lines → 2ⁿ locations (16 → 64 K). Address bus one-way; data bus two-way.
• Flags: zero, carry, sign, overflow.
theory.Addressing modes: • Immediate: operand in instruction. Direct: address in instruction. Indirect: address of address (two memory accesses). Register / register-indirect. Indexed: arrays (base + index). Relative: PC + offset (branches). Base register: relocation. Auto-increment/decrement: stepping through arrays.
theory.Instructions:
• 0-address = stack machine; 1-address = accumulator; 2/3-address = general registers.
• RISC: simple fixed-length instructions, load/store, many registers, hardwired, pipelined. CISC: complex, variable length, microprogrammed.
theory.Control unit: • Hardwired: fast, hard to change. Microprogrammed: control memory holds microinstructions; flexible, slower. Horizontal (wide, one bit per signal) vs vertical (encoded).
theory.Memory:
• Hierarchy (fast → slow): registers, cache, main memory, disk. Cache works on locality (temporal, spatial); built from SRAM; main memory DRAM (needs refresh).
• Mapping: direct (one line), fully associative (any line), set associative (any line in a set). Address = tag | line/set | offset; offset = log₂ block size, line = log₂ lines.
• AMAT (hierarchical) = h·tc + (1 − h)(tc + tm). Write-through vs write-back (dirty bit).
• RAM volatile; ROM, flash non-volatile.
theory.Pipelining:
• k-stage, n instructions: (k + n − 1) cycles; speedup = nk/(k + n − 1) → k.
• Hazards: structural (resources), data (dependencies; forwarding), control (branches; prediction, delayed branch).
theory.I/O:
• Programmed I/O (polling), interrupt-driven, DMA (CPU only sets up; burst / cycle stealing).
• NMI cannot be masked; vectored interrupts give the ISR address.
theory.Arithmetic:
• Booth's algorithm: signed multiplication. Restoring/non-restoring: division.
• IEEE 754: single 1/8/23 bias 127; double 1/11/52 bias 1023.
